content:
Apologies if this isn't quite the correct channel for this, but I was wondering if there's a kind of standard way of doing this for those papers citing lots of external results, or your own external certificates? I'm using codex to automate most of the lean code for my project, and it's building huge pipelines and at least trying to verify things coming from the certificate mean what they say they mean, but it's a lot harder trying to reproduce someone else's paper's external certificates. Is it accepted to just axiom external results like that? I hate leaving the uncertainty that something is wrong and it's just hidden behind a certificate issue, or worse it doesn't fulfill the exact requirements of the external theorems

https://github.com/kimihiro64/Robin is my current example
No, it's terrible idea to use axiom for external results. It's in practice highly unreliable, and no one is going to trust what you write if you do this. Sorry, but this is why we build libraries!

Kim Morrison said:

No, it's terrible idea to use axiom for external results. It's in practice highly unreliable, and no one is going to trust what you write if you do this. Sorry, but this is why we build libraries!

I mean particularly for things where there's a lot of finite computation backing up the result, but the result itself is a trusted theorem that just hasn't been added to mathlib yet because of its reliance on those external tables/finite computations. It's not particularly easy/efficient to do actual computations in lean from what I've seen so far, so when you need large scale (100k+ values checked), how should you handle it? Or when the precision required needs arbitrary precision, or arb ball arithmetic, etc.
This is essentially a research project / open territory, and there are not great examples to point you to.
There are some projects which rely on either native_decide or automatic axioms created by delegating to computer algebra packages (e.g. sympy)

• PrimeCert is an example of fully verifying computational stuff in Lean
  • I think LeanCert uses native_decide, and PNT+ relies on it
  • lean.py provides by sympy, and also some interface with z3
My Polychromatic project also uses C++ and Z3Py to do finite computations, then validate them in Lean, so the final theorem uses no native_decide.
